# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Optical Baseline and SAR Backscatter
The Sentinel-2-only model serves as the primary baseline for this thesis. Its performance on the test set confirms the findings of the preceding project work [@klaver2025]: pixel-based machine learning models using temporal differences in vegetation indices, particularly NDII and NDVI, can detect mowing events with high accuracy when cloud-free imagery is available. The selection of 7 features through permutation importance analysis, down from the original 20, demonstrates that the mowing signal in optical data is concentrated in a small number of spectral change indicators. The remaining features, including raw band values and several vegetation index variants, contribute little additional discriminative power. The preceding study showed that reducing to even only one feature (e.g. $\Delta NDII$) can still achieve reasonable performance, but the inclusion of a few complementary features improves the detection of edge cases.

The GRD backscatter features, in contrast, showed negligible predictive value for mowing detection at this study site. The GRD-only configuration achieved near-random performance, and adding GRD features to the optical baseline did not significantly improve classification accuracy. This outcome is consistent with the findings of De Vroey et al. [-@devroey2021], who reported that SAR backscatter alone is a weak predictor of mowing events due to the confounding influence of soil moisture, precipitation, and phenological variation on the returned amplitude signal. While backscatter changes after mowing are physically expected, particularly a decrease in VH due to the loss of canopy volume scattering, these changes are small relative to the environmental noise floor and do not produce a reliable classification signal at the pixel level.

## Coherence as a Complementary Feature
The integration of interferometric coherence derived from SLC data produced a measurable improvement over the optical baseline on the coherence-eligible subset of events. The S2+CohJumps configuration, which combines the seven optical features with only the VV and VH coherence jump, achieved one of the the highest test-set F1-Score among all configurations.

The coherence jump features capture a physically distinct aspect of the mowing signal that is not accessible through optical data: the change in temporal phase stability caused by the removal of vegetation. This complementarity explains why the combination improves over either modality alone, even though the coherence-only model performs poorly in isolation. The weak standalone performance of coherence is attributable to the limited temporal resolution of the coherence signal (6 or 12-day baselines), the spatial resolution difference (20 m versus 10 m for optical), and the relatively low separability of mowed and unmowed coherence distributions at this site. 

These results align with the broader pattern observed in the literature. Reinermann et al. [-@reinermann2022] found that combining Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 for mowing detection in Germany actually reduced the F1-Score due to increased false positives. The present study avoids this outcome by restricting the SAR contribution to the two most informative coherence features rather than including the full set of backscatter and coherence variables. This suggests that the fusion strategy matters as much as the data sources themselves: selective feature integration based on empirical importance analysis outperforms indiscriminate combination.

## VH Coherence Inversion
A notable finding of this study is that the VH polarisation coherence jump behaves contrary to expectations from the literature. Tamm et al. [-@tamm2016] reported that both VV and VH coherence increase after mowing, as the removal of tall grass reduces temporal decorrelation. At the Zurich Airport study site, however, VH coherence was found to decrease after mowing for the mowed class, while VV coherence behaved as expected.
**[Note: add sentence with specific Cohen's d values and direction for both polarisations, referencing the relevant figure or table in results section.]**

Several factors may contribute to this inversion. The airport grasslands are managed under strict operational protocols that differ from the agricultural grasslands studied by Tamm et al., with potentially different grass species, cutting heights, and mowing frequencies. The C-band radar wavelength of approximately 5.6 cm interacts with vegetation structures at a scale where cross-polarised (VH) scattering is particularly sensitive to canopy geometry. It is possible that the specific vegetation structure of short airport grass after mowing produces a scattering environment where VH decorrelation increases rather than decreases, for example due to exposed soil surface roughness or residual vegetation patterns that differ from agricultural stubble. The SNR correction amplified rather than resolved this inversion, indicating that the effect is not an artefact of thermal noise contamination but reflects a genuine site-specific scattering response. 

This finding has practical implications for model design. The coherence jump features in the machine learning model capture the combined VV and VH signal without assuming a specific direction of change. The classifier can therefore learn the site-specific response pattern from the training data, regardless of whether it matches theoretical expectations. This data-driven flexibility is an advantage over threshold-based detection approaches that assume coherence increases uniformly after mowing.

## Effect of Spatial Postprocessing and threshold calibration
The spatial postprocessing methods were applied to address the salt-and-pepper noise characteristic of pixel-based classification. The impact of postprocessing on model performance should be interpreted in terms of the precision-recall trade-off: morphological operations and SLIC aggregation are expected to remove small isolated false positive detections (improving precision) but may also eliminate small true positive regions at the edges of mowing polygons (reducing recall). 

The threshold calibration process was crucial for translating the model's probabilistic outputs into actionable binary predictions. The LOO-calibrated threshold ensured that the model's performance was optimised for the specific characteristics of the operational scene, balancing the trade-off between false positives and false negatives before full deployment and postprocessing.

## Limitations
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the results of this study.
The model was trained and evaluated exclusively on grasslands at Zurich Airport. Airport grasslands are managed under specific operational protocols and may not be representative of agricultural or ecological grassland management in other regions. The extent to which the model generalises to other sites, grass species, and management regimes remains untested beyond the preliminary qualitative assessment on external patches described in @sec-results.

The ground truth data were recorded by airport operations staff and reflect planned mowing schedules rather than precise spatial documentation of actual mowing extent. The quality and spatial accuracy of these records directly affect both model training and evaluation. Despite efforts to acquire additional ground truth from external institutions, no datasets with the required spatial and temporal resolution were obtained, limiting the study to a single reference source.
 
The coherence features were available for only 33 of the 63 training events due to incomplete SLC processing. This reduced sample size for Group B configurations limits statistical power and means that the comparison between S2-only and S2+coherence models operates on different subsets of the data. Furthermore, the absence of Sentinel-2 data for 2022 creates a gap in the temporal coverage that affects both training data availability and the assessment of year-to-year consistency. 

The coherence rasters were computed at 20 m resolution and resampled to 10 m to match the optical grid. This resampling introduces spatial smoothing and means that the coherence features do not capture sub-20 m spatial variability. The mismatch in native resolution between the optical and SAR features is a structural limitation of combining these two sensor types.

## Outlook
Large data collection with very much larger quantities of precise and more diverse ground truth data.
